The '''Laguerre–Pólya class''' is the class of [[entire function]]s consisting of those functions which are locally the limit of a series of polynomials whose roots are all real.
<ref>[http://www.intlpress.com/MAA/p/1999/6_1/MAA-6-1-021-038.pdf "Approximation by entire functions belonging to the Laguerre–Pólya class"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081006131503/http://www.intlpress.com/MAA/p/1999/6_1/MAA-6-1-021-038.pdf |date=2008-10-06 }} by D. Dryanov and Q. I. Rahman, ''Methods and Applications of Analysis'' 6 (1) 1999, pp. 21–38.</ref>
Any function of Laguerre–Pólya class is also of [[Pólya class]].

The product of two functions in the class is also in the class, so the class constitutes a [[monoid]] under the operation of function multiplication.

Some properties of a function <math>E(z)</math> in the Laguerre–Pólya class are:
*All [[root of a function|root]]s are real.
*<math>|E(x+iy)|=|E(x-iy)|</math> for ''x'' and ''y'' real.
*<math>|E(x+iy)|</math> is a [[non-decreasing function]] of ''y'' for positive ''y''.

A function is of Laguerre–Pólya class if and only if three conditions are met:
*The roots are all real.
*The nonzero zeros ''z<sub>n</sub>'' satisfy

:<math>\sum_n\frac{1}{|z_n|^2}</math> converges, with zeros counted according to their [[multiplicity (mathematics)#Multiplicity of a root of a polynomial|multiplicity]])

* The function can be expressed in the form of a [[Hadamard product (entire functions)|Hadamard product]]

:<math>z^m e^{a+bz+cz^2}\prod_n \left(1-z/z_n\right)\exp(z/z_n)</math>

with ''b'' and ''c'' real and ''c'' non-positive. (The non-negative integer ''m'' will be positive if ''E''(0)=0. Note that if the number of zeros is infinite one may have to define how to take the [[infinite product]].)

==Examples==
Some examples are <math>\sin(z), \cos(z), \exp(z), \exp(-z), \text{and }\exp(-z^2).</math>
<!--What about the Bessel function J0?-->

On the other hand, <math>\sinh(z), \cosh(z), \text{and } \exp(z^2)</math> are '''''not''''' in the Laguerre–Pólya class.

For example,

:<math>\exp(-z^2)=\lim_{n \to \infty}(1-z^2/n)^n.</math>

Cosine can be done in more than one way. Here is one series of polynomials having all real roots:
:<math>\cos z=\lim_{n \to \infty}((1+iz/n)^n+(1-iz/n)^n)/2</math>
And here is another:
:<math>\cos z=\lim_{n \to \infty}\prod_{m=1}^n \left(1-\frac{z^2}{((m-\frac{1}{2})\pi)^2}\right)</math>
This shows the buildup of the Hadamard product for cosine.

If we replace ''z''<sup>2</sup> with ''z'', we have another function in the class:
:<math>\cos \sqrt z=\lim_{n \to \infty}\prod_{m=1}^n \left(1-\frac z{((m-\frac{1}{2})\pi)^2}\right)</math>

Another example is the [[reciprocal gamma function]] 1/Γ(z). It is the limit of polynomials as follows:
:<math>1/\Gamma(z)=\lim_{n \to \infty}\frac 1{n!}(1-(\ln n)z/n)^n\prod_{m=0}^n(z+m).</math>
